segments.speaker: Diane Ineza · Host, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: Welcome to the second day of the YouthConnekt Africa Summit 2026 and the Future of Job plenary session. Good afternoon, I am Inenza Diang, your host from UNDP Rwanda. To set the scene, Rwanda's Ministry of Youth and Arts, in partnership with UNDP, carried out a youth forecasting exercise, looking at what work will look like for young people in 2035.

Here is a three-minute video to just see and look at what they have found, some of the findings. We've been struggling to relate AI to our practices. We believe that our routines, our schedules are always manual things.

However, from this training, I've been able to see how to integrate it. Apologies for that. And as they're looking for the video, after this video, there will be a question, a poll that you're going to have.
So have your phones ready, and we're going to have a poll. All right, let's move on. Now to open our second day, we'll come back to that.

To open our second day for the YouthConnekt Africa Summit 2026. In this session, mesdames et messieurs, chers jeunes, veuillez accueillir le ministre de la Jeunesse et du Sport de la République du Mali, monsieur Abdul Kassim Ibrahim Fumba. Ladies and gentlemen, please put your hands together for the Minister of Youth and Sport of the Republic of Mali.

Good morning, everybody. Monsieur le directeur du Centre Régional des Services du PNUD, excellents chers ministres et partenaires du développement, jeunes entrepreneurs, innovateurs et acteurs phares de notre continent. Bonjour et bienvenue à cette séance plénière de haut niveau du Sommet YouthConnekt Africa 2026.

Le conseil que le président Paul Kagame a adressé directement à la jeunesse africaine devrait guider nos discussions de ce matin. Il a dit, je cite, cessez d'attendre la permission et libérez-vous de cette mentalité qui consiste à attendre la validation de l'extérieur. Travaillez dur, gardez les pieds sur terre et le monde vous attendra.

Pour illustrer ce conseil en action, permettez-moi de vous raconter une petite histoire, celle de la jeune génération africaine d'aujourd'hui, symbolisée tout à l'heure par une performance artistique. Imaginez une jeune diplômée, ici même en Afrique de l'Est. Elle a fait des études, elle a acquis des compétences et elle tient entre ses mains une enveloppe qui représente son avenir professionnel.

Pendant des décennies, la seule question que nous nous posions en regardant cette enveloppe était quels emplois s'offriront à elle. Aujourd'hui, cette jeune femme, tout comme des millions de ses pairs à travers le continent, a décidé de ne plus attendre que quelqu'un lui ouvre la porte. Elle a brisé le seau de l'enveloppe pour poser une question bien plus audacieuse.

Qui mettra en place les systèmes qui permettront aux emplois de demain d'atteindre leur plein potentiel? Cette histoire témoigne d'un changement de paradigme fondamental. Comme le rappelle le thème de notre sommet, il s'agit de définir la mission d'une génération. Mais pour mener à bien cette mission, nous devons affronter la réalité de front, avec lucidité et pragmatisme.

Les données issues du récent exercice de prospective sur l'avenir de la jeunesse menée ici au Rwanda nous offrent un aperçu saisissant des défis et des opportunités auxquels notre continent est confronté. By 2050, Africa's population is expected to reach nearly 2.5 billion, about one quarter of the world's population, up from about 1.5 billion today. According to UN projections reported by PopulationPyramid.net, the population is projected to be around 2.47 billion, with a median age of approximately 25.4 years.

Nearly 60% of Africa's population will be under 25 years old in 2050, with fertility rates remaining high, particularly in West and East Africa. Nearly 70% of the population could be living in cities by 2050, placing significant strain on infrastructure, housing and public services. Artificial intelligence, digital transformation, the green economy and the creative industries are redefining the very nature of work.
This is the heart of our meeting today. As well-known African proverb says, if you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, let's go together.

To go far between now and 2035, we must stop viewing young Africans as mere job seekers awaiting an uncertain future. They are already entrepreneurs, innovators and builders. We have with us this morning champions who prove this every day, whether by connecting workers to stable jobs through data, building Africa's digital sovereignty via the local cloud or inventing clean cooking technology for our rural communities.

But their talent cannot flourish in an international vacuum. Access to financing, open regional markets, appropriate infrastructure and responsive public policies are the essential foundation for unlocking this potential. Today, we are not here simply to state the obvious.

We are here to address a central question together. How can young Africans, governments, businesses and development partners join forces to build the economies, institutions and opportunities that will shape the future of work by 2035? I invite you to listen, to debate, but above all, to take action so that we can not only prepare young people for the future of work, but also empower them to create it. Thank you and I wish you an excellent plenary session.

Thank you very much, Roland. Africa is a young continent, and Rwanda is no exception. 3.78 million young people are aged between 16 to 30 and more than 244,000 finish school and start looking for work every year.

Work is changing fast. AI, digitalization and the green transition are opening new opportunities in ICT, manufacturing, climate smart agriculture and platform one. They also bring risks of job displacement and skills mismatches.

The challenge is ensuring young people have the skills and opportunities to benefit from these transformations. To understand what this could mean by 2035, Rwanda used economic models, a thousand simulations and the voices of young people themselves. The first finding is simple.
Growth alone is not enough. For every 1% of growth, youth employment grows by less than half a percentage. But the study also shows what makes a difference.

In Rwanda's data, young people with technical and vocational certificates have nearly three times the odds of formal work. Investment in ICT, manufacturing and agro-processing creates more jobs where skills are in place. Finance without collateral, childcare and inclusion open more doors.
Gig workers need basic protection and AI readiness belongs in training now. Young people are already moving. Gig and platform work almost tripled in two years.

They are building and the system needs to catch up. Rwanda is not alone in facing these challenges. South Africa funds sector training through an employer levy and has proposed a national unit to turn labour market data into training decisions.

Kenya uses channeling funds to back informal enterprises, including those led by women and youth with disabilities, and digital tools to modernise farming. Its gig economy shows both the opportunity and the need for protection. Different systems, one shared challenge.

Connecting skills, jobs and finance. The scenarios to 2035 are not predictions. They show that when skills, investment, finance and inclusion move together, the outlook is stronger than on the current path.
Rwanda's findings, alongside lessons from South Africa and Kenya, point to one message. The future of jobs depends on the systems we build today. The question belongs to all of us.

What are we building for the young people entering our labour markets? And you continue to answer and you hold on that thought. We'll come back in to it at the end. We have had the honourable minister.

segments.speaker: Diane Ineza · Host, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: We have had the video. Now let's hear the same question told through art. Please welcome Mashirika with the envelope.

A generation with purpose has a question in waiting. A question that's passed on every time a new African star is born. It's true, times are changing, pacing, challenging our strengths and limitations.
And so every generation ponders on how they too can leave our continent a better place than they found it. Look. Where? Over there.
Here? No. What? Yes. Look beyond your current circumstance, they say.

And so we search, high, low, in and out, rummaging through a society that often bombards us with misinformation, opinions and several directions. When will I get a job? I do have a job. It's not the kind of job you're used to, but it's definitely working, right? Oh, no.
Oh, no. Not again. What I thought would work is challenging me to look deeper, closer.
I trade across borders 24-7 and I have never, ever once had to attend a physical meeting. I have a degree and an online store. I sell nails, hair and shoes.
Once your lash is done, send me a DM and book an appointment. That's how we roll over here. I'm a freelancer committed to a single mission, holding the future of Africa.
Learned everything I know from YouTube University. Hi there. I grew up in London, but Cairo is my home.

And I want to make an impact where it matters the most. We might have different backgrounds, cultures and pathways, but are brought together by one single question. We're not waiting to be rescued, but what can we do today to strengthen the future of Africa's workforce? My mind is restless.
Pacing, dreaming, thinking, searching for my purpose. Opportunities to learn new skills, deepen and apply them. Years of experience, I experience real life every day.
Searching, creating, building. But where does the search end and the point of creation begin? Pressure to stay relevant keeps mounting. I need to make a change and turn my potential into prosperity.
Through the noise, build, build, build and reconnect. Break, break, break that block. Bridge, bridge, bridge every gap.
Break, break, break through the noise. Build, build, build and reconnect. Break, break, break that block.
Bridge, bridge, bridge every gap. Ideas transmitted beyond borders, but it starts with you. You have the spark, the flame, the vibe.
Your mind is a workshop. Tinkering, learning and adapting. Your hands crafting, connecting.

Imagine the capacity of not just one, but of all. So think to yourself, where can you be of service? Where can you apply your insights and knowledge? Where can your uniqueness bring the most value? If I build the system, who sustains it? I do. If you sustain the system, then who anchors it? She does.
If she anchors the system, who evaluates, reimagines and improves it? We do. We all do. It's our shared responsibility.

Time to put those dreams into action and shape the generational mission. We are one continent. your excellencies, honorable ministers, distinguished guests, allow me to welcome again the countries represented here.

Cameroon, Kenya, Uganda, Lesotho, Gabon, Benin, Madagascar, Mali, Sierra Leone, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Chad, Liberia, Burundi, Sudan, South Sudan, Gambia, Gambia, Botswana, Guinea, Ethiopia, Burkina Faso, Nigeria, Congo, Angola, Malawi, are you there? Central Africa, Tanzania, Namibia, Seashell, last but not least, Rwanda.

segments.speaker: Diane Ineza · Host, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: Now to take us, to take our conversation further, please welcome the Forever Young, the Director of the UNDP Region Service Center for Africa, Dr. Matthias Knab. Please put your hands together for Chief Knab.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: I didn't hear Ghana, but I am here. Your excellency, the Right Honorable Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Lesotho, Your Honorable Minister of Mali, Excellence Abdul Kassim Ibrahim Fumba, Ministre de la Jeunesse chargée de l'instruction civique et de la construction citoyenne, other honorable ministers from across the continent, excellencies, ambassadors, members of the diplomatic corps, my fellow UNDP senior leadership present here, distinguished development partners and private sector leaders, my fellow young people, can we hear you loud and clear? It looks like the energy is not loud enough. Can we try again? Young African leaders, entrepreneurs and innovators, ladies and gentlemen, good morning.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Bonjour. It is an honor to join you on behalf of the UNDP administrator who would have wished to be here himself in person. And it's indeed a joy for me to be back in Kigali.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: I used to work here many years ago, a city that I call home. Our young performers who just left really did an excellent job of putting a question in our minds. And I hope we all understood that question.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: And we need to find an answer to that question. And the question is, who will build the systems that let the work to count? And in that envelope, I am still wondering what is in that envelope. Africa has the world's youngest population, yet millions of young Africans still struggle to find decent and productive work.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: While artificial intelligence, digital transformation and the green transition reshape what work looks like. Our challenge is not only to prepare young people for the jobs of tomorrow, it is to build economies capable of creating those jobs. And therefore, ladies and gentlemen, allow me to highlight only three priorities.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: First, job creation belongs at the heart of Africa's economic transformation. Rwanda has already made that choice, committing to 250,000 decent and productive jobs every year. Its recent youth forecasting exercise shows what that ambition will demand.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Nearly four in ten employed young people are overqualified for their jobs, and they earn about half as much as those whose skills match their work. Education is moving faster than the economy's ability to absorb it. And skills remain essential, but they need to be matched by productive investment, entrepreneurship and access to markets.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Growth alone does not automatically create enough decent jobs. Therefore, the quality of that growth matters just as much. The second priority, young entrepreneurs are already building Africa's future, and they need backing at scale.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: They need supportive ecosystems, access to finance and markets, and policies that let their businesses grow. Through YouthConnekt and Timbuktu, UNDP works with governments and partners to strengthen those ecosystems. Again, I would like to thank the European Union in particular, whose support through Aguka is helping young Rwandans turn ideas into businesses.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Ladies and gentlemen, the third priority is what is already working must now be built on together. Governments, businesses, investors, partners and young people need to build the systems that let young people's work count. Finance does not depend on collateral they do not have.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Skills that employers recognize, markets that reach across borders, and protection for those working on platforms and in the gig economy. Above all, young people should be recognized not as beneficiaries, but as partners in shaping Africa's economic future. That includes young women who still face the steepest barriers to decent work.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Excellencies, distinguished participants, Africa's future of jobs will be shaped by the choices we make today, the investments we mobilize, the institutions we strengthen, and the opportunities we open. So who will build those systems? All of us, and young Africans belong among the builders not waiting at the end of the line. UNDP remains committed to working alongside governments, the private sector, our partners, and Africa's young innovators to turn this generational opportunity into decent jobs, inclusive growth, and lasting prosperity for all.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: I thank you for your kind attention.

segments.speaker: Diane Ineza · Host, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Naab, and I'll bring you back just very soon. Yesterday, young people asked the questions.

segments.speaker: Diane Ineza · Host, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: Today, they will share the answers they are building already. But first, let's meet them. Rachel, Jean-Luc, and Tafara, I'll let them introduce themselves.

segments.speaker: Diane Ineza · Host, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: A round of applause to our young champions. Over to you, Rachel. We can't do better for her.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Your excellencies, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: My name is Rachel Obande, and I'm Zambian, proudly Zambian. And I am an aspiring wildlife manager, and I co-founded, I'm a co-CEO of Green Roots Innovation Limited. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: Thank you. So Green Roots Innovation Limited is a women-led, youth-led organization that I co-founded with my partner. And we promote land restoration, climate smart agriculture, as well as energy, as well as cooking technologies that are clean and sustainable.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: Now, have you ever visited a village or a rural area? And have you ever found women or girls using firewood for cooking? And have you ever wondered how they keep that fire burning? And one of the women who used this technology for cooking was my grandmother, who I held so dearly in my heart. And when I visited her time to time in the village, we would go in the woods in order to take firewood for cooking. And she would explain to me all the time that the forest had been going further and further away from her home, and it has been hard for her.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: She had backaches. And she would tell me time and time again that females, as well as women and young girls who went to take firewood, used to be harassed and taken advantage of. And one question that I had in my head was, how can I make life very easy for my grandmother? And that is how we promoted the double burner twig stove at Green Roots Innovation Limited, a sustainable stove that uses twigs, briquettes, as well as pellets to function.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: But one challenge that we had was that we did not have engaged the community properly. And we understand that for you to provide a solution into the community, they are supposed to accept it and feel that it is ours, and they are part of the solution that you're building for them. And that is what Green Roots Innovation Limited has been working on.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: And I'm glad to share with you that in 2025, we piloted six stoves in district, central province, Zambia, with the help of the Mukuba Unipod. And currently in 2026, we have worked by producing 60 stoves that over half has been sold. And that is our story for Green Roots Innovation Limited.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: So from this, we took it into our hearts that we must be the people, we are the opportunities to create jobs, and we are the people to create solutions. And if you want to connect with me after this session, I'll be available to show what we have from Green Roots Innovation. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: Have a seat.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: Your excellencies, honorable ministers, dear distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, my name is Sauve Jean-Luc. I was born and raised in Kigali.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: And ever since I was young, I was fascinated by the power of computers. I even have scars on my hand that I got from getting electrocuted when I was playing with computers at the age of five. 11 years later, I was admitted and got a scholarship at Randa Coding Academy.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: This is a school which was an initiative by the Ministry of ICT in partnership with other government institutions. From the education I got there, it led me to landing my first job as a software engineer in senior five, which is an equivalent of grade 11. And in the consecutive years, I got opportunities to work in some of Randa's biggest institutions as a software engineer, and for some, I was even leading the development team.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: After graduating there, I was admitted to the African Leadership University. That is where I met four of my former Randa Coding Academy colleagues. And we shared a sentiment.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: We shared a strong belief that Africa, Randa and Africa as a whole should be technologically independent, especially in this information age, especially in this age of AI, where data sovereignty is now more important than ever. We should have control of our own data. A lot of our data in Randa and in the continent is stored and processed outside the continent.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: And we are paying millions of dollars for that. So our question was, why? And that is why we built StretchCloud. We built StretchCloud to stand as the AWS of Africa.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: We built StretchCloud to stand as the Google Cloud of Africa. We built StretchCloud to stand as the Microsoft Azure of Africa. And our vision is not only to be like them, do what they're doing, but eventually become the leaders of technology, become the pioneers of emerging technologies.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: StretchCloud today is serving more than 250 software development teams across startups, SMEs and corporates in fintech, health tech, e-tech and many other sectors. Recently, StretchCloud was selected among the top 10 in Hanga PitchFest around the whole country. We are yet to know who the top five will be.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: And the finale is next week. I hope you will all be there. But in addition to that, and beyond that, I hope everyone in this room will join us, will join StretchCloud in the journey of making Africa technologically independent.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: Hello, YouthConnekt. It's such an honor to be back.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: My name is Tafara Makaza. I'm originally from Zimbabwe, but I'm based in Kigali. My very first time, thank you.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: My first time in Kigali was actually in 2019, where I was part of the YouthConnekt Africa boot camp. And since then, I went back to university to finish my studies in astrophysics. And then I graduated in 2022, but I couldn't stop thinking about the opportunities that were on the continent.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: I'm sure for a lot of you who are in Kigali for the first time, you've seen how clean the city is. And a lot of that is because of the people that clean every day. And for me, I couldn't help thinking about those people that clean those streets every day in terms of, you know, what does the future look like for them, right? What does a resume look like for them? What does a pension look like for them? So that led me to stop thinking about astrophysics and problems in the sky, and to start focusing on solving problems that are on the ground.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: So I moved back to Kigali to co-found a company called Fixa. And I will tell you a little bit about Fixa. So as we heard earlier, Africa has a lot of young people.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: And year on year, we have a lot of these young people that are entering the labor market. But unfortunately, we cannot create enough formal jobs to sort in these young people that are getting into the labor market. So as a result, a lot of these young people end up working in industries such as agriculture, manufacturing, construction, and mining.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: And a lot of that work is quite informal, and it's also done on pen and paper. So with Fixa, our solution was quite simple. We essentially work with the largest employers in labor-intensive industries.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: We give them a payroll software, which then allows them to pay their workers on time. And then we utilize all that data to build digital career identities for the workers, and also to make them access financial services. You can think of it as a LinkedIn for the linked out.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: And you can think of Fixa as that layer that enables people that traditionally were not able to access formal services to now be able to build their lives into the future and have that identity. I am really grateful to be here today because, of course, I did start my journey with YouthConnekt. I am also one of the alumnus of Generation 17, which is a partnership between Samsung and UNDP to work with young people that are helping solve the global goals.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: I'm really excited for this conversation, and I'm looking forward to really talk about how we are building this future of work, because it's not going to be handed to us. Thank you. Another round of applause for all our young leaders.

segments.speaker: Diane Ineza · Host, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: I'm going to invite Dr. Nab on the floor again. Please welcome. So while they talk, you can also join.

segments.speaker: Diane Ineza · Host, UNDP Rwanda
segments.text: There will be questions that will come on the screen, and over the few minutes that are remaining, three questions will appear on the screen. One of the time, please, I will invite you, if you have something to say, you will join it. Over to you.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Thank you very much, moderator. And can we give a round of applause to these fantastic young people up here with me? I was asked to come back because I think my colleagues wanted to have an intergenerational dialogue. And I protested because they want me to look old here and to be talking to young people, but I refuse.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: We are all young, aren't we? Yes, we are. Fantastic. So you all have very beautiful stories that are very inspirational.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: And given the time constraints, I had developed a lot of questions for you so that you could share with colleagues about what drove you to start and what is your future ambition in terms of contributing your quota to solving Africa's problems and also giving opportunity to young people. But then, with time constraints, I will give one question to each and every one of you. And please try to go straight to the point.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: And if time allows, we may ask for one more question from the crowd as well. Let me start with my sister here. Rachel.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Yes, director. Through Green Roots Innovation, you have experienced both opportunities and challenges of developing and introducing new technologies. Could you highlight one or two barriers preventing young green entrepreneurs from scaling their innovations into sustainable businesses? And what should governments do? I want you to focus on what governments should do because we have quite a number of honourable ministers here, including the right honourable prime minister.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: What do you expect from them to do to help you address those challenges that you face? Thank you very much, director. Thank you, everybody.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: One of the barriers and one of the challenges that I mentioned is community stakeholder engagement.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: And surprisingly, most young people take it lightly, especially when they are trying to introduce a product in the market. We must understand that it is very important that we put in the people and engage them in the solution that we want to produce and what we want to provide for them. The other barrier, as well as the other challenge that I would like to address here today is the challenge of transitioning from a small startup business to a successful one.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: Currently, we had experienced an issue where we would have money coming in, but I studied wildlife management and we're still working on that. We have been working on trying to engage the government as well as our leaders to give us mentorship because financing that we have been receiving through grants, through policies that have been given to us young people, is that mentorship has been taken away. And what do I mean by that? We need mentorship on how to manage our money and finances, how to put in back our profits back into the business, and how we can grow our money.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: So we need financial literacy in business relations. As well as business mentorship and financial mentorship. And we need them with us because we need it.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: As well as Green Roots Innovation, I speak to our Zambian government, our Zambian ministries, Ministry of Sports and Arts, that we need mentorship. Thank you. Can we give her a round of applause please? That was very clear.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: The need for stakeholder engagement as a critical challenge because you are developing a product for the community. And if you don't engage them before, during, and after, the product could actually not be used. And you talked about the need or the challenge of transitioning from a startup into a successful venture and business where you take it to scale and also continue to create jobs for people.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Now, the call to action is to our Ministry of Youth and Sports in Zambia. And you have a fantastic minister whom I sure has heard you loud and clear for mentorship, financial literacy, and also issues around, you know, even access to finance, isn't it? Yes. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Can we give her a round of applause please? Let me go to my astrophysicist, now trying to solve problems on the ground. Technology and AI are often presented as threats to employment. And based on your experience, can technology create more and better jobs for African youth, particularly those working in the informal sector? I decided to take this question because you came from the sky and now you're on the earth.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: So let us take it forward. You want me to repeat the question? Oh, that's fine. Am I audible? Yeah.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: Yeah. Thank you. That's a great question.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: Technology is an enabler. It's an opportunity. And I think we're living in unprecedented times in terms of AI and access to technology, right? Just like a few decades ago, we leapfrogged straight into mobile phones, right? Internet access.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: I think for me, the biggest barrier, especially when it comes to employment, which goes to what I was mentioning, is really just that digitization, right? A lot of the majority, like the majority of the workforce on the continent, is still invisible because they are managed quite on pen and paper. They are already working. We just have to add that layer of visibility.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: And when we have that layer of visibility, I think the Honorable Minister mentioned that we cannot build the future of work in an institutional vacuum. So with that visibility, we can then work with public institutions to give them insights for them to make better policies. For example, we do that here with the Ministry of Labor.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: We can work with, say, the Social Security Board to give people access to pension because of that visibility. We also work with financial institutions to give them non-collateralized loans because they have that data to know how much money people are making. So the informal economy, that's such a tricky word to use.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: A lot of these workers are working. It's just that most of them are quite invisible. And technology, especially in the year of 2026, is quite accessible.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: And you can literally build a lot of things that would take a year in a fraction of the time, which is quite an opportunity today.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Fantastic. Can we give a round of applause to Tafara? So the fact that we are seeing the positive side of technology, which is basically using it as an enabler, we can actually take advantage of it to be able to transition most of our informal sector colleagues through digitization and bring them and make them visible.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Excellent. But I also heard you talk and refer to the case of Rwanda, where you're working with the Ministry of Labour and others, which also comes back to a call to action to our ministers right in front here, that for us to be able to move the needle forward, we have to ensure that our government ministries, our government policies are all in line in supporting moving people from the informal sector to the formal sector, making them visible, and then using technology as an enabler. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: And Nyakubawa, Jean-Luc, you have a fascinating story which you shared, and I hope that the electrocution that you had when you were five, all five-year-olds will be very clever to not be electrocuted. Now, that said, you are building a cloud technology company in Rwanda, or you have already built Stretch Cloud, in a sector that many would traditionally associate with large international technology companies. You mentioned them.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: You gave us a little bit of your experience, but I would like you to tell us more, your experience about Africa's potential to create its own technology-driven jobs and industries.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: Thank you very much, Honorable Director. That is a very good question.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: I believe I have a strong belief that in this age of AI, it's taking us to a very positive future, an age of what we would call the age of abundance. And we will reach there because we will only be harnessing the part of the technologies we have at hand to the best of our abilities. I believe that Africa, especially its young people, will play a very key part and role in creating those opportunities.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: I gave myself as an example. I got an education from all of the educational institutions that I got, I had, but the introduction of AI was a very good timing because it was like a lot of knowledge at our hands that was near that we could harness. And we managed to build something that would have taken more than two years before the introduction of AI, LLMs, and it took us only three to four months to launch our product.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: And it was already in the market. And this is not only the opportunity where the technology that we have right now could be used for. We have a lot of places that still need automation.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: There is healthcare. And I believe that in the future, we're going to move from the software to physical things, things we can touch, robotics, chemists who are going to be using AI to discover new drugs to cure diseases, and many much more. So I think this is going to be an opportunity if and only if the young people of Africa puts the opportunities that we have on it and use it at the best of our ability.

segments.speaker: Jean-Luc · Kigali
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Thank you very much. Can we give them all a round of applause? Let me check with my colleague what time we have left.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Do we have some more time? Ten minutes. Ten minutes. Oh, less than that.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Fantastic. No, let's give them a round of applause. And while I make them think about the last question where I will ask each one to just share an opinion, one minute.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: And the last question for all of you is, imagine Africa in 2035. What new types of jobs do you believe young people could be doing that are not yet widely available? You hinted on that, but I would like to hear others as well. So think about it.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: But in the meantime, we do have the Honourable Prime Minister from Lesotho here, who from yesterday and today, I'm told, has been in business for more than 40 years. Your Honourable Prime Minister, I would like you to, if I may indulge, to share maybe a two-minute experience of how these young people could grow their businesses. My sister from Zambia says they need to learn how to manage their money.

segments.speaker: H.E. Samuel Matekane · Prime Minister of Lesotho
segments.text: He also talked about how there are other opportunities out there for young people. So if we could get the microphone to the Right Honourable Prime Minister from Lesotho. Thank you very much, Moderator.

segments.speaker: H.E. Samuel Matekane · Prime Minister of Lesotho
segments.text: Like I said yesterday, business is all about patience. You first start, you take your time to see the returns, but the most important thing in business is to plough back into business. And the other mistake that I've realised is that we, as the owners of business, we always tend to give us a higher salary.

segments.speaker: H.E. Samuel Matekane · Prime Minister of Lesotho
segments.text: That is wrong. Try to sacrifice as much as possible so that you keep business going. Business can actually make you, but you just have to be patient.

segments.speaker: H.E. Samuel Matekane · Prime Minister of Lesotho
segments.text: Every business is a good business, especially when you give it a chance to grow. I know that most of the time we are saying we are in a hurry to see the returns. No, business does not cater for that.

segments.speaker: H.E. Samuel Matekane · Prime Minister of Lesotho
segments.text: We all have to give business time to grow. It will take you a few years before you can really see some returns or probably dividends, but you have to give it time. So patience, be a patient patient, so that things can go your way.

segments.speaker: H.E. Samuel Matekane · Prime Minister of Lesotho
segments.text: Especially some good returns, because that is what you will see at the end of the day. Good rewards, because you'll be earning through your own sweat. That is when you'll start seeing returns.

segments.speaker: H.E. Samuel Matekane · Prime Minister of Lesotho
segments.text: But I must also say to our young entrepreneurs, our young African entrepreneurs, I've been in business for the last 40 years. It took me time, a long time, to see that I've really made it. So that I'm a typical example of how business should be handled.

segments.speaker: H.E. Samuel Matekane · Prime Minister of Lesotho
segments.text: Let's take our time. One day we will all smile to the bank and we will be able to buy any car that you want. I always tell them that cars have got first names and surnames.

segments.speaker: H.E. Samuel Matekane · Prime Minister of Lesotho
segments.text: You have the likes of Rolls-Royce, Aston Martins, Cayenne, Porsche. Those are the cars that you'll later be able to acquire them. Even with not without the assistance of the banks, you can be able to swipe them with your own credit card.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Your Excellency, the Right Honorable Prime Minister. This is very helpful.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: And coming from you who has been there, done that, I think it has answered some of the questions that the panelists here were actually alluding to. So the Prime Minister says every business is a good business. So there is no bad business.

Secondly, we all need patience and the fact that we need to plow back, invest whatever profits we're making into growing the business to scale. And I think this is very useful advice for us young people who are venturing into business. Good.

So we now have a minute each to the last question I asked. Imagine yourself or imagine the year 2035. And what new types of jobs do you believe young people in Africa could be doing that are yet not available now? We start with you and then we go to my sister, the last voice.

Yes, again, that's a very good question. I believe that in 2035, most of the jobs that we'll be having are the jobs that we can barely name right now. But if I will try my best to predict, I'll say in two key sectors.

The one is the one that I mentioned before, physical AI. We're going to need to automate as much physical processes as possible. We're going to need affordable smart houses, which will increase our productivity and security.

We are going to need to have our systems of security, security of our cities and countries automated as much as possible. So it is now the right time to understand the core science behind how things work. People who are learning physics, chemistry, biology, so that they will use in addition to the power of AI with the knowledge that they have to build and create those solutions.

And second is the research and development. I believe that in the upcoming year, there's going to be a race of small groups of R&Ds that are working together to find out solutions that have never been there, to put them out there on the market, which are the solutions that are only going to come out of the research and intensive development. And third, which is the last, I believe most importantly, is the skill to stay adaptable, is the skill to stay flexible and to change when the change is needed.
Because either way, we will need to change, but we will change either by will and to change before or we will be dragged along the process when it is inevitable to change. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Thank you very much, Jean-Luc.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: You spoke like a futurist, taking us to the future. Thank you very much. Tafara? Yeah, I second what Jean-Luc said.

segments.speaker: Tafara Makaza · Co-Founder, Fixa
segments.text: I'll also speak as an optimist. So there is a number that, you know, was thrown that, you know, year on year, the number of working age, you know, people in Africa is going to continue to grow. I'll also flip that to say even the number of people that are retiring is going to grow, right? So if you look at today, if a majority of those people are working in this informal economy, if you now go into 2035, you have to think about what does, you know, pension look like for them, what does healthcare look like for them, what does banking look like for them, and all those are opportunities that we can start building right now.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Yeah. Thank you very much, Tafara. And to the last panelist, Rachel, give us your futuristic view of where jobs will be created.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: Thank you very much, Director. Thank you very much, everybody. So currently when you go to my country, Zambia, and some parts of Africa, you will find households still using the three-stone open fire cooking solution, using wood as fuel, and still using charcoal, which is still on high demand.

segments.speaker: Rachel · Green Roots Innovation, Zambia
segments.text: But in the future, 2035, I see green technology, I see sustainable technology, I see the transitioning from using firewood for cooking, from using charcoal for cooking, from cutting down trees to something smarter. I see women building, I see them producing clean cook stoves, I see them making briquettes, clean biomass for them to use to protect the planet, to protect themselves, and to protect their health. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: Thank you. No, thank you very much, Tafara, Rachel, and Jean-Luc. This has been a very, very inspiring conversation, very instructive in the way you all have inspired all of us here.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: And I would just like to say that the last question remains very optimistic. You all gave a very optimistic view of the future, linking it to the opportunities that will be created. But those opportunities also come with some challenges, or what I call problems.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: And it is those problems that young people will be looking forward to solving that will create the jobs that we are looking for, for young people. Now, imagining research and R&D as part of something that would help us solve some of those problems, and then also the fact that you mentioned automation, that is interesting to look at that. I was beginning to think automation, and I'm thinking maybe then I'll be able to even predict when everything is going to happen in my own village.

segments.speaker: Dr. Matthias Naab · Director, UNDP Regional Service Centre for Africa
segments.text: And last but not the least, the optimistic view by Tafara, also looking at how we'll be solving issues around pension, healthcare in the future. And last but not the least, Rachel looking at green technologies taking over the market space in the interest of saving our planet. Thank you very much to all of you.
Can we give them a round of applause? There'll be just a photo, and then we continue another round of applause for them. A group photo. We're going to put back the question we asked at the start.
We're going to see. Okay. The question was, what is the biggest barrier to young people accessing decent work in your country? I think insufficient job opportunities is winning here.

That's what the poll is saying. And the second one was, in one word or two, what's the biggest opportunity for young people in your country by 2035? And you say technology. There is a bit of digital entrepreneurship and opportunity, job, AI, innovation.
All right. And the third one, what's one thing you want leaders to do now? And I see you seek about coming. The beauty of this poll.
I want leaders to invest in young people by creating more opportunities for education, employment, and entrepreneurship. All right. I like that you are engaging with the conversation.
Our business leader says job. Wonderful. And another question we asked you.
By the way, these polls and these questions are going to stay on. If you still want to engage, please go on. And yes.

So the next one, it was about which sector do you believe has the greatest potential to create jobs for young people, for young African people by 2035? And 43% of you say digital economy and AI. And 26% said agriculture and agro-processing. Oh, it's reducing.
Okay. All right. Keep it up.
It's your voices. I think someone is changing their mind. Yeah.
Oh, I see. Digital economy and AI. These are all information that our excellencies and honorable ministers and leaders here that are keeping in mind.
I think those are all the questions that we had. And oh, yes. So the question we started was who will build the system that lets the work count? And the answer is all of us.

So merci beaucoup, your excellencies, honorable ministers, distinguished guests, young African leaders, thank you very much. It's been my pleasure to host you. And thank you for honoring our invitation.
Thank you to the government of Rwanda and the European Union, our partners for Agukai Initiative. And thank you everyone again. I hope that the DJ will usher us out.

Thank you very much. Ladies and gentlemen, young leaders, honorable ministers, excellencies, we have a session coming at 11.30 that will be dedicated on buy from youth. So please don't run away from us.
It will be a very interactive, interesting session. Please stay with us. We have a session coming from buy from youth in the agri-food system.
So please, those who want to join us, you're welcome. Thank you. Thank you.
